newsitem.title: RUSSIA: War-weary Chechens fight poverty, pin hope on poll.
newsitem.headline: War-weary Chechens fight poverty, pin hope on poll.

text.p: Bek Halimov points to piles of rubble by the roadside and gives a fatalistic shrug.

"Just look at this mess. Whoever takes charge in Chechnya will have a hell of a job putting things back together again," said the former Soviet collective farm agronomist who now makes a living changing money at the bazaar in war-ravaged Grozny.

Two weeks on Monday, on January 27, the million-strong region will elect a new president and local assembly. Yet four months after a ceasefire ended 21 months of war between Chechen rebels and Russian troops much of the province lies in ruins.

In Grozny, once a tranquil Caucasian capital of 400,000, many buildings are without windows, doors or roofs, their walls still scarred by shells and bullets -- graphic testimony to the pounding it endured early in the war and again last August.
Power cuts are common and running water erratic. Few telephones work and senior officials, businessmen and journalists communicate almost exclusively by satellite 'phones.

With much of its Soviet-era industry, including lucrative oil refining, destroyed, unemployment is put at anywhere between 60 and 90 percent. But there are no official statistics and many people get by on trading and wheeler-dealing.

"I earn just $10 a day changing money here, which buys a few kilos (pounds) of meat, and I have five children to support," said Halimov. His broad smile is typical of a people resilient in the face of adversity. By Russian standards, though, his income is not quite desperate poverty.
Despite the complaints of local people, the bazaar, which defiantly carried on throughout the war, is surprisingly well stocked with food, clothes, medicines and household goods.
But traders complain that few have money in their pockets.

"Business is very bad, worse than during the war," said Madina Govrgayeva, hawking a range of items from cosmetics to pens at her small roadside stall. While the Russian army ran the town, she could count on soldiers spending their pay.
Local people are pinning their hopes on the elections. Under the peace accord with Russia these polls are the first step in restoring order and stability in the Caucasian territory.
Five main candidates all support Chechen secession from the Russian Federation. But some traders expressed concern over the economic consequences of a move likely to anger Moscow.
"If we declare independence Russia may close the roads and business will be even worse," said trader Asya Akhmedova.
But the defiance that sustained Chechnya's plucky fighters against Moscow's armed might is never far from the surface.

"It is better to die honourably than to be part of Russia. We want nothing to do with Russia. I want recognition of my right to exist as a citizen of a free country," said Daniil Malik, an unemployed construction engineer also changing money.
Despite a high level of interest in the elections, the campaign remains fairly low key, due mainly to lack of funds.
Cars and shop windows carry posters featuring the main presidential candidates, usually depicted against the backdrop of Chechnya's green, white and red striped flag.
The best organised candidate, former information minister Movladi Udugov, has published leaflets detailing his political programme, which includes a market economy.
The candidates have also started holding rallies across the mainly Moslem region. People turn out in large numbers to cheer on their favoured candidate despite icy weather and muddy roads.

"These elections are essential to reestablish law and order in Chechnya and to give state power democratic legitimacy," said Grozny-based Tim Guldimann of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which is observing the polls.
"The people here are working hard to ensure that they go ahead properly. They want them to succeed," he told Reuters.
Echoing his words, the traders in the bazaar said they were keen to vote and let the long task of reconstruction begin.
"The election holds our hopes. We need order and peace again in our land," said bearded bookseller Bislan.
